events.title: Beethoven's Ninth Premieres
events.blurb: A nearly deaf 53-year-old composer, standing on the podium while a co-conductor did the actual directing, premiered a vast hour-long symphony that broke with convention by adding four vocal soloists and a chorus to the orchestra in its final movement. The text was a Schiller poem celebrating universal brotherhood. At the end the composer had to be turned around by one of the singers to see the audience — which he otherwise could not hear — thundering applause.
events.revealBlurb: May 7, 1824 — Ludwig van Beethoven at the Theater am Kärntnertor, Vienna. He had been profoundly deaf for over a decade. The "Ode to Joy" theme is now, somewhat jarringly given the text, the official anthem of the European Union.

events.title: Rhapsody in Blue Premieres
events.blurb: A 25-year-old former Tin Pan Alley song-plugger's first major concert work — a one-movement concerto for piano and jazz band — premiered at a Manhattan concert hall advertised as "An Experiment in Modern Music." The piece's opening clarinet glissando, improvised in rehearsal as a joke, was left in. The concert had begun with banal novelty pieces; by the time the composer walked out to sit at the piano, the audience was dozing. He woke them up.
events.revealBlurb: February 12, 1924 — George Gershwin at Aeolian Hall, Manhattan. The bandleader was Paul Whiteman. The audience included Rachmaninoff, Stravinsky, Fritz Kreisler, and Sergei Rachmaninoff. United Airlines has used it as its ad music since 1987.

events.title: Strange Fruit Recorded
events.blurb: A 23-year-old African-American singer, in a Manhattan studio, recorded a song about the lynching of Black Americans that had been written by a Jewish high-school teacher from the Bronx. Her regular label refused to release it; a tiny specialty label agreed. She closed with it at every set at her Greenwich Village club, the room going dark except for a spotlight on her face, no encore permitted. The song haunted her for the rest of her short life.
events.revealBlurb: April 20, 1939 — Billie Holiday, Commodore Records. Songwriter: Abel Meeropol, under the pen name Lewis Allan. Meeropol and his wife later adopted the two young sons of the executed Ethel and Julius Rosenberg.

events.title: Dylan Goes Electric
events.blurb: A 24-year-old folk singer, backed by a ragged rhythm section from the previous night's acquaintance, walked onto the stage of a folk festival on a Rhode Island pier with a sunburst Stratocaster slung low over his shoulder. He played three short electric songs before some boos drowned out the applause. He walked off, returned with his acoustic, and played two more. The event marked, depending on who tells it, the birth of folk-rock or the betrayal of American folk.
events.revealBlurb: July 25, 1965 — Bob Dylan at the Newport Folk Festival. Pete Seeger, legend says, tried to cut the sound cables with an axe. Seeger later denied it. The songs included "Maggie's Farm" and "Like a Rolling Stone." Dylan's next tour was booed nightly for a year.

events.title: MTV Launches
events.blurb: A new American cable channel devoted entirely to music videos went on the air at one minute past midnight Eastern time with a countdown, a rocket, and a footage loop of the Apollo 11 moon landing with the channel's logo hoisted as a flag. The first music video it played was a novelty track by a British synth-pop group with a prescient title. Within four years it had reshaped the music industry's priorities and, quite possibly, a generation's attention span.
events.revealBlurb: August 1, 1981 — Music Television. First video: "Video Killed the Radio Star" by the Buggles. The channel ran music videos almost exclusively until the late 1990s; today it runs reality programming and airs barely any music.

events.title: First Networked Email
events.blurb: A computer engineer working for a Cambridge, Massachusetts research firm sent an electronic message between two computers sitting next to each other in his office, using a symbol from the typewriter keyboard he'd picked precisely because it was never used in names — the "at" sign — to separate the user name from the host machine name. He could not recall years later what the message had contained; probably "QWERTYUIOP" or similar.
events.revealBlurb: October 1971 — Ray Tomlinson at BBN Technologies. The @ symbol's adoption was arbitrary but lasting. Tomlinson's contribution is the reason your email address contains an @. He died in 2016.

events.title: First Website Goes Live
events.blurb: The first webpage to be publicly accessible on the internet was posted from a workstation in a Swiss laboratory. It explained what the World Wide Web was, how to set up a web server, and how to use a web browser. Its URL ended in ".ch"; its creator had built the whole stack — browser, server, editor, protocol — in about a year and a half.
events.revealBlurb: August 6, 1991 — info.cern.ch, by Tim Berners-Lee. The original page was lost at one point; CERN restored a 1992 copy in 2013. The server, a NeXT workstation, is still on display with a sticker reading "DO NOT POWER DOWN — THIS IS A SERVER."

events.title: Google Incorporated
events.blurb: Two Stanford PhD students filed articles of incorporation for a search-engine company they had been developing in a dormitory and a rented garage in suburban California. Their algorithm, unlike those of competitors, ranked pages by how many other pages linked to them. They would never graduate. Their search index contained 60 million pages when they incorporated; it contains hundreds of billions today.
events.revealBlurb: September 4, 1998 — Larry Page and Sergey Brin. The name is a misspelling of "googol," the mathematical term for 10^100. Their initial financial backer, Sun Microsystems co-founder Andy Bechtolsheim, wrote a $100,000 check to "Google Inc." before the company formally existed.

events.title: Snapchat Launched
events.blurb: Three Stanford undergraduates released an iOS app that let users send photos that automatically disappeared a few seconds after being viewed. One founder had pitched the idea for a product-design class the previous spring and been told it was terrible. The app would grow explosively as a teenage-first social platform and introduce "Stories," a format quickly copied by every major competitor.
events.revealBlurb: September 26, 2011 — Evan Spiegel, Bobby Murphy, and Reggie Brown. Originally named Picaboo. Facebook offered to acquire Snap for $3 billion in 2013; Spiegel said no. Snap went public in 2017 at a $24 billion valuation.

events.title: TikTok Launches Globally
events.blurb: A Chinese short-video company merged its existing lip-sync-focused app Musical.ly, acquired the previous year, into a new global brand — effectively introducing mainland China's most popular short-video format to Western audiences. The app's algorithm would prove uniquely good at inferring what content users wanted without asking them. Within three years, TikTok had over a billion users and had reshaped every other social platform's product roadmap.
events.revealBlurb: August 2, 2018 — ByteDance merges Musical.ly into TikTok. By 2020, U.S. users were spending more time per day in TikTok than in Instagram or Facebook. President Trump attempted to ban it in 2020; the Biden administration attempted to force a U.S. divestment in 2024.

events.title: Jesse Owens Wins First Berlin Gold
events.blurb: An American sprinter from Alabama won the first of four gold medals at the Berlin Summer Games, finishing the 100-metre dash in 10.3 seconds before 110,000 spectators. He went on to win gold in the 200 metres, long jump, and 4×100-metre relay — shattering the narrative that the host nation's athletes would dominate.

events.title: Jesse Owens at Berlin Olympics
events.blurb: A 22-year-old African-American sprinter won four gold medals at a Summer Olympics held in the capital of a regime that had publicly declared the inferiority of his race. He took the 100m (10.3), 200m (20.7), long jump (8.06m), and 4×100m relay. His performance personally refuted Nazi racial theorizing on a stage the regime had built for its own glorification. He was welcomed home with a ticker-tape parade through New York but had to ride a freight elevator at his own Waldorf-Astoria reception because Black guests were not permitted in the main elevators.
events.revealBlurb: August 3-9, 1936 — Jesse Owens. The story that Hitler refused to shake his hand is disputed; Hitler had stopped shaking any medal winners' hands after the first day. President Roosevelt never congratulated Owens; Owens said later: "Hitler didn't snub me — it was our president who snubbed me."

events.title: Black Power Salute in Mexico
events.blurb: Two African-American sprinters, having just won gold and bronze in the 200 metres at a Summer Olympics, stepped onto the medal podium shoeless, wearing black socks, and raised black-gloved fists as the U.S. national anthem played. The Australian silver medallist on the second step wore an Olympic Project for Human Rights badge in solidarity. The gesture — a deliberate human rights protest — cost the two Americans their Olympic careers; they were suspended from the U.S. team and booed on their return home.
events.revealBlurb: October 16, 1968 — Tommie Smith and John Carlos; the Australian was Peter Norman. Norman was subsequently ostracized by the Australian team; the two Americans bore his pall at his 2006 funeral. A 7-metre statue of the podium moment stands today on the San Jose State University campus.

events.title: Phelps Wins 8 Golds in Beijing
events.blurb: A 23-year-old American swimmer won his eighth gold medal of a single Summer Olympic Games — surpassing Mark Spitz's 36-year-old record for most golds in a single Olympics. He set or broke world records in seven of the events. His final gold came in the 4x100m medley relay. Over four Olympic Games he would win a career total of 23 golds and 28 total medals, more than any athlete in any sport before him.
events.revealBlurb: August 17, 2008 — Michael Phelps at the Beijing Olympics. Spitz's previous record was 7 golds from 1972 Munich. Phelps's career gold total eventually reached 23; he retired after Rio 2016. Spitz had been a rumored spectator at many of Phelps's events.

events.title: Kobe Bryant Dies
events.blurb: A 41-year-old retired basketball star, his 13-year-old daughter, and seven other passengers died when their private helicopter crashed into a hillside in thick fog outside Los Angeles while en route to a youth basketball game. The retired player had won five NBA championships, two Olympic golds, and the nickname "Black Mamba" during a 20-year career entirely with the Los Angeles Lakers. The crash prompted an outpouring of mourning around the world.
events.revealBlurb: January 26, 2020 — Kobe and Gianna Bryant. National Transportation Safety Board findings attributed the crash to pilot error in poor visibility. His 2017 jersey-retirement ceremony at Staples Center saw both his numbers (8 and 24) raised to the rafters — the only player in franchise history with multiple retired numbers.

events.title: Teapot Dome: Senate Investigation Opens
events.blurb: The Senate launched its first formal investigation into the Teapot Dome oil fields that autumn, following revelations that Interior Secretary Albert Fall had secretly leased federal naval petroleum reserves in Wyoming and California to private oil companies in exchange for personal cash loans and gifts totaling roughly $400,000. Fall would become the first U.S. Cabinet member ever convicted of a crime committed while in office.
events.revealBlurb: October 1923 — Washington, D.C. The oil companies that paid the bribes — Sinclair Oil and Pan American Petroleum — were acquitted at trial; only the man who took the bribes was convicted. President Harding died of a heart attack in August 1923, before the scandal fully broke.

events.title: Scopes "Monkey Trial" Begins
events.blurb: John T. Scopes, a high school teacher in Dayton, Tennessee, went on trial for violating a state law banning the teaching of human evolution in public schools. The case — which pitted famed defense attorney Clarence Darrow against three-time presidential nominee and Christian fundamentalist William Jennings Bryan — was broadcast nationally on radio and drew journalists from across the country to the small town.
events.revealBlurb: July 10, 1925 — Dayton, Tennessee. The trial was deliberately staged by the town's businessmen to attract tourists and publicity; Scopes wasn't sure he had actually taught evolution. He was convicted and fined $100, but the verdict was overturned on a technicality. Bryan died five days after the trial ended.

events.title: Atomic Bomb Dropped on Hiroshima
events.blurb: At 8:15 that morning, a B-29 Superfortress named the Enola Gay released a uranium bomb nicknamed "Little Boy" over the Japanese city of Hiroshima, which detonated at 1,968 feet above the city center with a force equivalent to approximately 15,000 tons of TNT. Estimates of deaths in the four months following the explosion range from 90,000 to 166,000; roughly two-thirds of the city's buildings were destroyed.
events.revealBlurb: August 6, 1945 — Hiroshima, Japan. "Little Boy" was the first nuclear weapon ever used in warfare, but it had never been fully tested — scientists were confident enough in the gun-type design. Japan did not surrender after Hiroshima; it took a second bomb (Nagasaki, August 9) to produce the surrender announcement.

events.title: Apollo 1 Launchpad Fire
events.blurb: During a ground test at Cape Kennedy that afternoon, a fire broke out inside the Apollo 1 command module, killing all three crew members — Gus Grissom, Ed White, and Roger Chaffee — in less than a minute. The cause was an electrical spark in an atmosphere of pure oxygen at elevated pressure, and the hatch could not be opened quickly enough to save anyone.
events.revealBlurb: January 27, 1967 — Launch Complex 34, Cape Kennedy, Florida. The crew could not escape because the hatch required 90 seconds to open inward — and the fire created pressure that made it impossible to swing. The disaster set the Moon program back 20 months but ultimately produced a safer spacecraft.

events.title: Nixon Resigns the Presidency
events.blurb: That evening, Richard Nixon became the first and only U.S. president to resign from office, delivering a nationally televised address from the Oval Office in which he announced his departure would take effect at noon the following day. The resignation came after the release of the "smoking gun" tape proved Nixon had personally directed the Watergate cover-up six days after the break-in, making his impeachment and Senate conviction certain.
events.revealBlurb: August 8, 1974 — The Oval Office. Nixon's approval rating the week of his resignation was 24%. Gerald Ford pardoned him one month later, saying "our long national nightmare is over" — a pardon that likely cost Ford the 1976 election. Nixon is the only president ever to resign.

events.title: Watt's Separate Condenser Patent
events.blurb: A Scottish instrument maker received a patent for a steam engine design that used a separate condenser chamber, dramatically reducing fuel consumption. Unlike earlier designs that wasted energy reheating the main cylinder on every stroke, the new engine converted roughly 75% more heat into mechanical work.

events.title: Liverpool-Manchester Railway Opens
events.blurb: The world's first inter-city passenger railway line opened with ceremony, carrying dignitaries including the Duke of Wellington on eight parallel trains along a 56-kilometre line linking the port of Liverpool with the cotton-manufacturing centre of Manchester. A parliamentary member, William Huskisson, stepped onto the tracks at a refueling stop and was struck by an oncoming locomotive. He died that evening — the first well-known railway fatality.
events.revealBlurb: September 15, 1830 — designed by George Stephenson. Huskisson is universally regarded as the first prominent casualty of the railway age, though he was not strictly the first railway death. The line ran horse- and steam-hauled freight alongside passengers for its first decades.

events.title: First Transatlantic Telegraph Cable
events.blurb: After two previous attempts failed mid-Atlantic, a joint American-British consortium successfully laid a 3,700-kilometre copper cable across the ocean floor between Ireland and Newfoundland. The Queen of England and the President of the United States exchanged the first messages. The cable's signal degraded rapidly — the 99-word inaugural message took 17 hours to send — and the cable failed entirely within three weeks, but the feasibility had been proved.
events.revealBlurb: August 5, 1858 — the cable was completed; August 16, the first messages between Queen Victoria and President James Buchanan. The project's main backer, American financier Cyrus West Field, persisted through four failed attempts and finally established a durable cable in 1866. His Atlantic cables cut communication between continents from weeks to minutes.

events.title: Bell Patents Telephone
events.blurb: A 29-year-old Scottish-born American inventor was granted a patent on "the method of, and apparatus for, transmitting vocal or other sounds telegraphically." Three days later he made the first recognized telephone call in his Boston laboratory, summoning his assistant from the next room. The patent, filed the same morning as a rival inventor's competing application, would become the most valuable patent ever issued by the US government.
events.revealBlurb: March 7, 1876 — Alexander Graham Bell. The first call: "Mr. Watson — come here — I want to see you." The rival, Elisha Gray, filed his caveat a few hours later; legal battles continued for years. American Telephone & Telegraph, founded on Bell's patent, became the largest corporation in the world.

events.title: Eiffel Tower Opens
events.blurb: A 300-metre wrought-iron lattice tower, built over two years, two months, and five days as the entrance arch to a Paris world's fair, was completed. At three times the height of the Washington Monument, it was the tallest man-made structure in the world and would remain so for 41 years. A petition signed by 300 prominent French artists had protested the "useless and monstrous" project during construction. It was intended to be demolished after 20 years; radio antennas saved it.
events.revealBlurb: March 31, 1889 — designed by Gustave Eiffel for the 1889 Exposition Universelle, marking the centennial of the French Revolution. It remained the tallest building until the 1930 Chrysler Building. The Nazi occupation cut the elevator cables; Parisians said the "Hitler had to climb the stairs to the top."

events.title: Battle of Crete
events.blurb: For the first time in military history, an entire island was invaded and captured primarily by paratroopers and glider-borne troops alone, dropped onto an enemy-held coastline in the face of fierce resistance. The attackers suffered such catastrophic losses on the opening day that the tactic was never repeated at this scale.
events.revealBlurb: May 20 – June 1, 1941 — Operation Mercury. German paratroopers suffered over 6,500 casualties, including roughly 3,000 killed. Hitler was so shaken he banned future mass airborne operations. The British, Australian, and New Zealand defenders were evacuated; 5,000 were left behind and taken prisoner.

events.title: Rosie the Riveter Campaign
events.blurb: A deliberate government and industry campaign to recruit women into heavy industrial and weapons manufacturing work portrayed a bandana-wearing figure flexing her arm above the slogan "We Can Do It!" alongside magazine illustrations that reached millions of households, reshaping public expectations of gender and labour across a nation at industrial-scale mobilisation.
events.revealBlurb: 1942–1943. The number of women in the US workforce rose from 12 million to 20 million — a 57% increase — by 1944. Women built B-29s, welded Liberty ships, and operated cranes. The Westinghouse "We Can Do It!" poster was seen by almost no one during the war; it was rediscovered in the 1980s and became an icon of the feminist movement.

events.title: Battle of the Bulge
events.blurb: 250,000 troops and nearly 1,000 tanks punched through the thinnest part of an Allied front in a snow-covered forested highland, achieving complete surprise and driving a 90-kilometre bulge into the line — the largest land battle ever fought by the United States Army, and the last major offensive Germany would ever launch in the west.
events.revealBlurb: December 16, 1944 – January 25, 1945. German soldiers wore American uniforms and used captured jeeps to spread chaos behind the lines; dozens were caught and executed. When the surrounded garrison at Bastogne was asked to surrender, Brigadier General Anthony McAuliffe replied with a single word: "Nuts!" The Germans had to ask for a translation.

events.title: Atomic Bombing of Hiroshima
events.blurb: A single aircraft flying at high altitude released a single bomb over a mid-sized city at 8:15 in the morning, detonating it 600 metres above a distinctive T-shaped bridge with the force of 15,000 tons of TNT — flattening 13 square kilometres, killing between 70,000 and 80,000 people instantly, and ultimately causing 140,000 deaths by the end of the year.
events.revealBlurb: August 6, 1945 — B-29 Enola Gay, piloted by Colonel Paul Tibbets, dropped "Little Boy" over Hiroshima. The aiming point was the Aioi Bridge. The bomb missed by about 250 metres but it did not matter. Tibbets's mother's name was Enola Gay. The co-pilot, Robert Lewis, wrote in his journal: "My God, what have we done?"

events.title: Atomic Bombing of Nagasaki
events.blurb: A second atomic strike, delivered three days after the first, detonated with the force of 22,000 tons of TNT over a city's industrial valley — but cloud cover over the primary target had forced the bomber to divert to its secondary, sparing one city and condemning another, while a city 160 kilometres away had been removed from the target list weeks earlier at the personal request of the American Secretary of War.
events.revealBlurb: August 9, 1945 — the B-29 Bockscar dropped "Fat Man" at 11:02 AM. Kokura, the original target, was obscured by clouds; pilot Sweeney diverted to Nagasaki. An estimated 40,000 died instantly; 80,000 total by year's end. Secretary of War Stimson had personally removed Kyoto from the target list because he had visited it on his honeymoon and loved it.

events.title: IBM Personal Computer Launched
events.blurb: A technology corporation released a personal computer based on an Intel processor running an operating system licensed from a small software company for $25,000. Its open architecture allowed third-party manufacturers to build compatible clones, spawning a global personal computer industry worth trillions within a decade.

events.title: IBM PC Released
events.blurb: The world's dominant mainframe computer maker released a small desktop machine built, unusually for the company, from off-the-shelf parts — an Intel 8088 processor, an operating system licensed from Microsoft, components any competitor could buy. Business customers trusted the name and bought millions. The design's open specifications led to a decade of "IBM compatible" clones that collectively made the Intel/Microsoft duopoly inevitable.
events.revealBlurb: August 12, 1981 — IBM PC model 5150. It had 16KB of RAM and no hard drive. IBM's decision to source DOS from Microsoft, rather than write it in-house, is usually cited as the great strategic error of 20th-century computing. Gates retained all distribution rights.

events.title: Deep Blue Beats Kasparov
events.blurb: An IBM chess-playing computer, running on a 480-processor supercomputer in New York and evaluating 200 million positions per second, defeated the reigning world chess champion in the sixth game of a six-game match. The loss — the first time a computer had defeated a world champion in a regulation match — the champion afterward accused IBM of cheating by having grandmasters intervene in the machine's moves, which IBM denied. IBM retired the machine immediately after the match.
events.revealBlurb: May 11, 1997 — Deep Blue vs. Garry Kasparov, New York. Final match score: 3.5–2.5 Deep Blue. The specific "intuition" move that shocked Kasparov (game 2, move 37) was later attributed to a bug in the code forcing a fallback routine.

events.title: Google Founded
events.blurb: Two Stanford doctoral students incorporated a search engine company whose name derived from the mathematical term for 10 to the power of 100. Their PageRank algorithm ranked results by treating hyperlinks as votes, producing more relevant results than the keyword-frequency systems that dominated at the time.

events.title: BlackBerry Released
events.blurb: A Canadian wireless technology company released a two-way pager with a small keyboard and a monochrome screen that could also receive email. Corporate IT departments loved it — executives could finally stay in touch while traveling — and within a few years the device had become a status symbol and, later, an addiction. Users typed with thumbs on the tiny QWERTY keys; the resulting repetitive-strain injury acquired the nickname "BlackBerry thumb."
events.revealBlurb: January 19, 1999 — Research In Motion's BlackBerry 850. Chosen name because the keyboard's buttons resembled the drupelets of a blackberry fruit. The iPhone's 2007 arrival began BlackBerry's long decline; RIM pivoted to BlackBerry Ltd. and left hardware in 2016.

events.title: Sistine Chapel Ceiling Unveiled
events.blurb: A 37-year-old Florentine sculptor, who had accepted a papal commission reluctantly after four years insisting he was not a painter, unveiled 500 square metres of freshly painted fresco covering the ceiling of a Vatican chapel. The work, which had taken four years, depicted nine scenes from Genesis surrounded by 300 figures. The artist had painted it while standing, not lying down as myth claims, his neck bent back for hours daily.
events.revealBlurb: October 31, 1512 — Michelangelo Buonarroti. He wrote a sonnet complaining of his neck: "I've grown a goiter by dwelling in this den… my beard turns up to heaven." Restoration between 1980 and 1994 revealed vivid colours under 400 years of candle smoke.

events.title: Magellan's Fleet Departs
events.blurb: Five ships and 270 sailors departed from Sanlúcar de Barrameda under a Portuguese navigator flying a Spanish flag, carrying provisions for two years. Three years later, one battered ship and 18 survivors returned — the first vessels to circumnavigate the globe, though their commander had been killed in a Filipino skirmish partway through.

events.title: Fall of Tenochtitlán
events.blurb: After a three-month siege — during which Spanish-allied Indigenous forces demolished the city district by district, channeled the causeways, and introduced a devastating smallpox epidemic — the last Aztec emperor surrendered in a canoe on the lake as his capital burned. The Spaniards, led by Cortés, renamed the ruins and built a viceregal capital on them. The Aztec empire ceased to exist; the Spanish conquest of the Americas was underway.
events.revealBlurb: August 13, 1521 — Cuauhtémoc surrendered to Cortés. The city's population had dropped from perhaps 200,000 to under 50,000 through disease, siege starvation, and fighting. The Spanish built Mexico City on the drained lakebed — which continues to sink today at 50 cm per year.

events.title: Drake Completes Circumnavigation
events.blurb: An English privateer, captaining one of five ships that had set out three years earlier on a raiding expedition against Spanish New World colonies, returned to his home port with holds full of Spanish silver and the honour of being the first Englishman — and second captain ever — to circumnavigate the globe. His queen personally knighted him on the deck of his ship. Spain's ambassador demanded his execution; the queen politely declined.
events.revealBlurb: September 26, 1580 — Sir Francis Drake aboard the Golden Hind at Plymouth. Only his ship of the original five returned, with 59 of the original 164 men. The queen's share of the plunder more than doubled her annual government revenue for that year.

events.title: Spanish Armada Defeated
events.blurb: A Spanish naval force of 130 ships and 26,000 men, intended to escort a Flemish invasion army across the Channel to England, was met by a faster, more maneuverable English fleet off the Flanders coast. An English fireship attack scattered the Spanish anchorage overnight; the following day's running battle crippled the armada. Storms in the North Sea and along the Irish coast destroyed the rest on the long retreat home. Barely half returned to Spain.
events.revealBlurb: July 29 to August 8, 1588 — Battle of Gravelines decided it. English commanders: Lord Howard of Effingham, Sir Francis Drake. Roughly 35 Spanish ships reached home; most of the rest were wrecked on the Irish coast, whose people dealt harshly with survivors.

events.title: Great Wall of China Begun
events.blurb: The first emperor of a unified Chinese state, having conquered the six rival warring kingdoms, ordered existing regional defensive walls in the north linked into a continuous frontier fortification against nomadic incursions. A conscripted army of 300,000 labourers worked for years; many died on the project and were, according to tradition, buried in its foundations. The Ming-dynasty wall, which is what most modern visitors see, was rebuilt over a millennium later.
events.revealBlurb: c. 220 BCE — Qin Shi Huang. The visible stone-and-brick wall is largely Ming-dynasty (1368-1644), built with much better materials. The Qin wall was mostly earthen and only fragments survive. Total length, across all versions, has been measured at 21,196 km.

events.title: Pont du Gard Built
events.blurb: A three-tiered limestone aqueduct bridge was constructed to carry water 50 kilometres across southern Gaul to the Roman colony of Nemausus (modern Nîmes). The top level — 48 metres above the River Gard — still carried its channel; the whole structure spans 275 metres. It was built dry, without mortar, using stones so precisely cut that the joints remain watertight after two millennia. The aqueduct itself was decommissioned in the 6th century; the bridge survived as a road crossing.
events.revealBlurb: c. 50 CE — built under Emperor Claudius. The water it carried had a gradient of only 1 in 3,000 — about 30 centimetres of drop per kilometre. The Pont du Gard is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site and one of the most visited tourist destinations in France.

events.title: Leaning Tower of Pisa Begun
events.blurb: Construction began on a free-standing bell tower for the cathedral complex of an Italian city-state on the Tuscan coast. By the time three of its eight stories were finished five years later, the soft alluvial ground beneath the south side was already sinking noticeably. Construction was halted for nearly a century. When work resumed, builders attempted to compensate by building upper floors taller on the low side — so the tower is actually curved. It was completed 199 years after ground-breaking.
events.revealBlurb: August 9, 1173 — Pisa Cathedral bell tower. The tilt is currently about 3.97 degrees after stabilization work completed in 2008. Galileo is said to have dropped balls of different weights from it to demonstrate they fall at the same rate — the story is almost certainly apocryphal.

events.title: Versailles Hall of Mirrors Completed
events.blurb: A French king's chief architect and royal painter completed the centerpiece of a vastly enlarged royal palace on the edge of Paris — a 73-metre-long gallery of 578 mirror panels on one side, facing 17 tall windows overlooking the palace gardens on the other, with a vaulted ceiling painted with 30 scenes of the king's military triumphs. Mirrors were at the time so expensive that a single pane could cost as much as a small estate; the gallery was a showcase of French glassmaking independence from Venice.
events.revealBlurb: 1684 — Jules Hardouin-Mansart (architect) and Charles Le Brun (painter) for Louis XIV. The Treaty of Versailles ending WWI was signed in the room on June 28, 1919 — a deliberate German humiliation in the same space where German unification had been proclaimed in 1871.

events.title: Panama Canal Opens
events.blurb: A 77-kilometre canal cutting across the narrowest part of the Central American isthmus opened to international shipping, after a US-run construction effort that had finished a French attempt abandoned two decades earlier amid malaria, yellow fever, and bankruptcy. The canal used a system of locks to raise ships 26 metres above sea level across the continental divide. It cut the sea route from New York to San Francisco by over 12,000 kilometres.
events.revealBlurb: August 15, 1914 — the ship SS Ancon made the first full transit. The American construction was made possible partly by controlling yellow fever and malaria through mosquito eradication. The 1977 Torrijos-Carter treaties returned the canal to Panamanian sovereignty in 1999.

events.title: Battle of Tours
events.blurb: A Frankish mayor of the palace led an infantry army into a defensive wall of shields against a much larger Umayyad cavalry force that had been raiding deep into western Europe. The battle's outcome stopped the northward expansion of the Islamic caliphate into the Frankish heartland and established the Carolingian dynasty as the dominant power of the region.
events.revealBlurb: October 10, 732 — Charles Martel ("Charles the Hammer") in central France. His grandson Charlemagne would be crowned emperor 68 years later. Edward Gibbon later wrote that without the victory, "the interpretation of the Koran would now be taught in the schools of Oxford."

events.title: Treaty of Verdun
events.blurb: Three grandsons of Charlemagne, after a three-year civil war, signed a treaty in a French town dividing their grandfather's empire into three kingdoms — a western Frankish one destined to become France, an eastern one destined to become Germany, and a middle strip whose ownership would be disputed for a thousand years.
events.revealBlurb: August 843 — Louis the German got the east, Charles the Bald got the west, Lothair got the middle (Lotharingia, surviving in "Lorraine"). The France–Germany border problem is essentially a 1,200-year-old inheritance dispute.

events.title: Battle of Agincourt
events.blurb: An exhausted English army, heavily outnumbered, caught in thick mud on a narrow front between two woods in northern France, stood behind sharpened wooden stakes and cut down the armored flower of French nobility with longbows at point-blank range. The French dead included a constable, three dukes, and over 1,500 knights; English losses were perhaps 400. Shakespeare would turn it into a speech 180 years later.
events.revealBlurb: October 25, 1415 — Henry V on St. Crispin's Day. Henry ordered the slaughter of prisoners mid-battle when he feared a rear attack; this remains controversial. The longbow's armor-piercing arrowheads were called "bodkins."

events.title: Siege of Orléans Lifted
events.blurb: A 17-year-old peasant girl from Lorraine, dressed in white armour and claiming visions from saints, led a French relief army into a besieged Loire Valley city. Over eight days of sorties, she personally led assaults on the English siege forts around the city, was shot through the shoulder with a crossbow bolt, returned to the fight, and broke the siege. The French war effort, exhausted for a generation, was transformed overnight.
events.revealBlurb: May 8, 1429 — Joan of Arc relieves Orléans. She had convinced a skeptical Dauphin to give her an army by passing a theological interrogation and, reportedly, a virginity test. She would see him crowned as Charles VII at Reims within ten weeks.

events.title: Gutenberg Bible Printed
events.blurb: A goldsmith in a Rhine-valley city completed the first book printed in Europe using movable metal type — a Latin Bible set in 42 lines per page, bound in 180 copies. His press combined existing technologies — oil-based ink, a wine-press frame, cast-metal punches — into an invention that would be blamed for everything from the Reformation to the Renaissance to modern literacy.
events.revealBlurb: 1455 — Johannes Gutenberg in Mainz. Forty-nine copies are known to survive; roughly twenty are complete. Gutenberg himself was sued by his financier the same year and lost the press.

events.title: Michelangelo's David Unveiled
events.blurb: A 29-year-old Florentine sculptor unveiled a 5.17-metre marble nude of a biblical hero, carved over three years from a single block of Carrara marble that had been rejected by two earlier sculptors as flawed. The statue was intended for the rooftop of a cathedral; a committee that included Leonardo da Vinci decided the work was too significant to put out of sight and instead installed it in the main square of the city.
events.revealBlurb: September 8, 1504 — Michelangelo Buonarroti. Moving it from the workshop to the Piazza della Signoria took 40 men 4 days. The statue was damaged by a mob in 1527 and by a 1991 attack with a hammer; it now stands indoors at the Accademia, where a copy watches over the piazza.

events.title: Raphael's School of Athens
events.blurb: A 28-year-old Umbrian painter completed the second of four monumental frescoes on the walls of the pope's private library at the Vatican, gathering the giants of classical philosophy into a single imaginary architectural space. Plato and Aristotle walk forward from a vanishing point; Pythagoras writes in a book, Euclid draws on a slate, Heraclitus leans alone on a block. The face of Euclid is the architect Bramante; Heraclitus is Michelangelo, working bitterly next door.
events.revealBlurb: 1511 — Raphael Sanzio, in the Stanza della Segnatura. The rivalry with Michelangelo, then painting the Sistine Ceiling a short walk away, was real; Raphael added him as an afterthought in a late revision.

events.title: Velázquez's Las Meninas
events.blurb: A court painter completed a 3.2-metre oil depicting a 5-year-old Spanish princess surrounded by her ladies-in-waiting, two dwarfs, a dog, and — impossibly — himself at his easel. A distant mirror on the back wall reflects the figures of her parents, the king and queen, who appear to be standing exactly where the viewer stands. The painting is essentially a visual puzzle about who is depicting whom and from where.
events.revealBlurb: 1656 — Diego Velázquez at the Spanish court. The princess is Margarita Teresa. Now in Madrid's Prado. Picasso painted 58 variations on it in 1957. Foucault opened his book The Order of Things with a long reading of its perspective.

events.title: David's Oath of the Horatii
events.blurb: A 36-year-old French painter, working in Rome, exhibited at the Paris Salon a sharply geometric, classically themed canvas of three Roman brothers swearing on their father's outstretched swords to fight for their city. Women wept in the shadows on the right. The painting's stark rejection of Rococo decoration and its austere civic virtue appealed exactly to the mood of a country five years from revolution.
events.revealBlurb: 1784 — Jacques-Louis David, exhibited at the Salon of 1785. Painted in Rome; shipped to Paris. David would become the leading painter of the French Revolution, personally designing the Tennis Court Oath as a commemorative picture and painting Marat dead in his bath.

events.title: Pollock's Drip Paintings
events.blurb: A 35-year-old American painter, working in a converted barn studio on Long Island, laid large unstretched canvases on the floor and moved around their edges pouring and flinging paint from sticks and hardened brushes. The resulting "drip paintings" rejected representational composition entirely in favour of overall visual rhythm. A 1949 Life magazine spread asked: "Jackson Pollock: Is he the greatest living painter in the United States?" and made him instantly famous and nearly famously alcoholic.
events.revealBlurb: 1947 — Jackson Pollock began the drip technique in Springs, NY. He died in a car crash driving drunk on August 11, 1956, aged 44. His "No. 5, 1948" sold privately in 2006 for $140 million, briefly the highest price ever paid for a painting.

events.title: Sargon of Akkad Founds the First Empire
events.blurb: A ruler of the city of Akkad conquered the independent city-states of Sumer one by one and then extended his control north and west into Anatolia, east into Elam, and possibly as far as the Mediterranean coast — the first time a single political authority had been imposed across all of Mesopotamia. He is said to have served as a cup-bearer before seizing power, and he ruled for 56 years. His empire was the largest the world had yet seen.
events.revealBlurb: c. 2334 BCE — Akkad, Mesopotamia. Sargon of Akkad (Sharrum-kin, "True King"). The location of his capital city has never been found by archaeologists. His legend — placed in a basket on a river as an infant, raised by a gardener — predates the Moses story by over a thousand years.

events.title: Epic of Gilgamesh Written Down
events.blurb: Five older Sumerian poems about a legendary king of one of the world's first cities were woven together into a single narrative — the oldest surviving long-form literary work. The epic follows a king and his companion through adventures, a great flood survived in a boat by carrying animals aboard, and the king's failed quest for immortality after his companion's death. Copies were made in royal libraries across the ancient Near East for the next thousand years.
events.revealBlurb: c. 1800 BCE — Babylonia (standard "Old Babylonian" version). The definitive 12-tablet version was assembled by a scribe named Sîn-lēqi-unninni around 1200 BCE. The flood tablet (Tablet XI), found in Ashurbanipal's library, caused a sensation in 1872 when George Smith recognized it paralleled the Biblical flood story.

events.title: Hanging Gardens of Babylon Constructed
events.blurb: A terraced garden structure of remarkable engineering — irrigated by a mechanical water-lifting system drawing from the Euphrates — was built within a palace complex in the world's largest city, reputedly to reproduce the forested hills of a queen's mountainous homeland in a flat river valley. The gardens required teams of workers to operate water screws continuously. They were later catalogued as one of the seven wonders of the known world.
events.revealBlurb: c. 600 BCE — Babylon (or possibly Nineveh). Attributed to Nebuchadnezzar II for his Median wife Amytis, but no Babylonian inscription confirms their existence. Oxford historian Stephanie Dalley has argued the gardens were actually at Nineveh, built by Sennacherib a century earlier, and the locations became confused.

events.title: Alexander the Great Enters Egypt
events.blurb: A Macedonian king was greeted at the eastern border of Egypt without military resistance, received at Memphis as a liberator from Persian rule, and ceremonially recognized as pharaoh. He then traveled west through the desert to consult the oracle at the Siwa Oasis, where he was reportedly proclaimed the son of the god Amun. Before departing Egypt, he marked out the boundaries of a new city on a narrow strip of land between the Mediterranean and a lake.
events.revealBlurb: Late 332 BCE — Egypt. Alexander III of Macedon. The city he founded — Alexandria — was officially laid out on April 7, 331 BCE, by architect Deinocrates of Rhodes. It would become the Mediterranean's greatest intellectual and commercial center within a generation.

events.title: Death of Cleopatra
events.blurb: The last active pharaoh of a civilization three thousand years old died in her palace in Alexandria after her naval forces were destroyed off the Greek coast and her partner had already fallen on his sword. She was the seventh ruler to bear that name and the first in her dynasty to bother learning the Egyptian language. Her death ended a kingdom founded by one of Alexander the Great's generals, and within weeks it became a Roman province.
events.revealBlurb: August 12, 30 BCE — Alexandria. The asp-bite story comes from Plutarch, writing 130 years later; modern historians favor a fast-acting poison. She spoke nine languages. Her kingdom, the Ptolemaic dynasty, had lasted 275 years.

events.title: Berlin Wall Construction Begins
events.blurb: East German soldiers and workers erected barbed-wire barricades along the full length of the border between East and West Berlin overnight, sealing the most visible escape route from the Eastern Bloc without advance public announcement. Within days, temporary barriers were replaced with concrete, dividing families who had crossed freely just the day before.

events.title: Partial Test Ban Treaty
events.blurb: Three nuclear powers signed a treaty in Moscow banning atmospheric, underwater, and outer-space testing of nuclear weapons — while carefully preserving their right to test underground. The agreement was driven partly by rising public alarm over radioactive fallout, which scientists had detected in the teeth of American children born far from any test site.
events.revealBlurb: August 5, 1963 — signed by the US, UK, and USSR. France and China, who weren't invited, kept atmospheric testing for years. Strontium-90 levels in baby teeth dropped sharply within a decade.

events.title: Prague Spring Invasion
events.blurb: Reform-minded leaders in a central European capital had spent eight months experimenting with "socialism with a human face" — easing censorship, rehabilitating purge victims, and tolerating debate. In the night, 250,000 Warsaw Pact soldiers and 2,000 tanks rolled across the borders. Unarmed civilians tried to argue with the invading soldiers; within days the reforms were reversed.
events.revealBlurb: August 20-21, 1968 — invasion of Czechoslovakia. Reformist leader Alexander Dubček was flown to Moscow and forced to sign a capitulation. A student named Jan Palach set himself on fire in Wenceslas Square five months later in protest.

events.title: Fall of Saigon
events.blurb: As enemy tanks crashed through the iron gates of the presidential palace in a Southeast Asian capital, U.S. helicopters lifted the last embassy staff and thousands of desperate local allies from rooftops around the city. The image of the final Huey ascending from an apartment building became the defining photograph of a failed 20-year war. Within hours, the city was renamed after a revolutionary leader who had died six years earlier.
events.revealBlurb: April 30, 1975 — the city became Ho Chi Minh City. The evacuation, Operation Frequent Wind, removed 7,000 people by helicopter in 19 hours. The famous "last helicopter" photo actually shows a CIA staff house, not the embassy.

events.title: August Coup Against Gorbachev
events.blurb: A committee of Soviet hardliners — the KGB chief, the defense minister, the vice president — placed the reform-minded Soviet leader under house arrest at his Black Sea dacha and announced on state television that he was "unwell." Three days of confusion followed. A reformist Russian president climbed atop a tank outside his parliament and defied the plotters. The coup collapsed in 60 hours, and so, effectively, did the union.
events.revealBlurb: August 19-21, 1991 — the tank-top defier was Boris Yeltsin. Gorbachev returned to Moscow to find his authority gutted; Yeltsin had eclipsed him. Within four months the USSR itself would be gone.

events.title: Sulla's March on Rome
events.blurb: When the Senate transferred his military command to a political rival, consul Lucius Sulla marched six legions across the pomerium — the sacred city boundary no Roman general had ever crossed in arms — and took Rome by force. It was the first time in the Republic's history that a sitting consul used his own army to seize the capital; most of his officers refused the order and resigned rather than obey.
events.revealBlurb: 88 BCE, Rome. After taking the city Sulla had his enemies declared public enemies, then left for his original campaign in Greece as if nothing unusual had happened. His opponent Marius promptly retook Rome, declared Sulla a criminal, and died of old age seven days into his seventh consulship.

events.title: Assassination of Julius Caesar
events.blurb: A group of Roman senators led by Cassius and Brutus surrounded the dictator in the Theatre of Pompey and stabbed him twenty-three times. A later physician concluded only one wound was fatal; the man fell at the base of a statue of his former rival, Pompey himself.
events.revealBlurb: The Ides of March, 44 BCE. Caesar had been warned by a soothsayer to "beware the Ides of March" and laughed it off the same morning. His last words, "Et tu, Brute?" come from Shakespeare — ancient sources quote him saying "You too, child?" in Greek.

events.title: Aurelian Reunifies the Empire
events.blurb: After the empire had fractured into three competing states, Emperor Aurelian defeated the Palmyrene Empire in the east — capturing its queen Zenobia — and then the breakaway Gallic Empire in the west, bringing Britain, Gaul, Spain, Syria, and Egypt back under a single ruler within five years of taking power. He then began building a massive new defensive wall around Rome itself.
events.revealBlurb: 274 CE. Queen Zenobia of Palmyra had claimed descent from Cleopatra and ruled a sophisticated court of scholars and poets while commanding legions across the Near East. After capture she was eventually settled near Tivoli and, according to some sources, married a Roman senator.

events.title: Council of Nicaea
events.blurb: Constantine convened roughly 220 bishops from across the empire in the city of Nicaea to resolve a theological crisis: whether Christ was fully divine or a created being subordinate to God, as the Arian faction argued. The council declared Arianism a heresy, defined Christ as "of one substance" with the Father, and produced the first version of the Nicene Creed — still recited in most Christian churches.
events.revealBlurb: May–July 325 CE. Constantine funded the bishops' travel, accommodation, and meals — the empire's first theological conference at state expense. He sat at the proceedings in purple and gold but had no vote. Despite the council's authority, the Arian controversy continued for another fifty years.

events.title: Battle of Adrianople
events.blurb: After Rome settled Visigothic refugees south of the Danube and then systematically starved and abused them, the Goths rose in revolt. Emperor Valens — who refused to wait for reinforcements — attacked their fortified camp with approximately 30,000 men. Gothic cavalry flanked both sides of the Roman line and trapped the legions; two-thirds of the eastern field army was destroyed and Valens himself was killed.
events.revealBlurb: August 9, 378 CE. Valens's body was never found. One account says he was carried wounded to a farmhouse, which Gothic soldiers then set alight; another says he was lost in the general slaughter. Military historians sometimes call Adrianople "the ancient world's Stalingrad."

events.title: Tchaikovsky's Swan Lake Premieres
events.blurb: A 36-year-old Russian composer's first full-length ballet score premiered at a grand theatre in the Russian capital, paired with choreography that was widely thought incompetent and dancing that was widely thought under-rehearsed. Critics focused their complaints on the music, which they found too "symphonic" for dancing. Only after the composer's death, in a restaged 1895 version with new choreography, did the ballet become a classic.
events.revealBlurb: March 4, 1877 — Pyotr Tchaikovsky's Swan Lake at the Bolshoi, Moscow (Old Style February 20). The 1895 St. Petersburg revival with Petipa/Ivanov choreography is the version most companies perform today. The tragic black-swan finale was a 1950s restoration.

events.title: The Rite of Spring Riot
events.blurb: A 30-year-old Russian composer's ballet score, depicting a pagan spring ritual with jagged rhythms, dissonant chord stacks, and primitivist choreography, premiered at a new Paris theatre and nearly caused a full-scale audience riot. Shouts, whistles, and fistfights broke out within minutes; the choreographer had to shout counts to dancers from the wings because they couldn't hear the orchestra. The piece is now considered one of the pivotal works of 20th-century music.
events.revealBlurb: May 29, 1913 — Igor Stravinsky and Ballets Russes at Théâtre des Champs-Élysées, Paris. Choreography by Vaslav Nijinsky. The Parisian critic Carl Van Vechten reported his seat-neighbour beating rhythmically on his head with his fists in distress.

events.title: Woodstock Festival Opens
events.blurb: A music festival on a dairy farm in upstate New York that had sold 186,000 advance tickets was overwhelmed by more than 400,000 attendees in the preceding 48 hours, forcing organisers to declare it a free event and abandon the ticket booths. Thirty-two acts performed over four rain-soaked days, and the festival became the defining cultural gathering of its generation.

events.title: Woodstock Festival
events.blurb: A three-day music festival, overcapacity within hours of opening, drew an estimated 400,000 young people to a dairy farm in upstate New York despite severe rain. Fences collapsed; the event became de facto free. 32 acts performed — Jimi Hendrix, Janis Joplin, The Who, Santana, Creedence Clearwater Revival, Joan Baez. Two people died (one from an overdose, one crushed by a tractor); two babies were born. The festival became the defining symbol of the 1960s counterculture.
events.revealBlurb: August 15-18, 1969 — on Max Yasgur's farm in Bethel, NY. Hendrix closed at 9 AM Monday morning to a dwindling crowd with a distorted, feedback-laced "Star-Spangled Banner." The 1970 documentary won an Oscar.

events.title: Nirvana's Nevermind Released
events.blurb: A three-piece rock band from the Pacific Northwest released their second album — recorded for $65,000, with a cover showing a naked infant underwater reaching for a dollar bill on a fishhook. The album's lead single had been written, according to the band, to sound "like the Pixies" and made a mockery of that idea. By January it had displaced Michael Jackson's "Dangerous" at number one and changed what major-label rock sounded like for the rest of the decade.
events.revealBlurb: September 24, 1991 — Nirvana, Kurt Cobain, Krist Novoselic, Dave Grohl. The lead single was "Smells Like Teen Spirit." The infant on the cover, Spencer Elden, later sued the band (unsuccessfully) for using his image.

events.title: Wagner's Ring Cycle Premieres
events.blurb: A 63-year-old German composer presented the first complete four-night performance of a 15-hour operatic cycle he had been writing, off and on, for 26 years, at a festival opera house in a Bavarian town he had specifically had built to host it. Audiences included Tchaikovsky, Liszt, Grieg, Bruckner, the emperor of Germany, and the emperor of Brazil. The complete run was a financial disaster.
events.revealBlurb: August 13-17, 1876 — Richard Wagner at the Bayreuth Festspielhaus, Bayreuth. The festival runs to this day; tickets are difficult to obtain. Wagner's anti-Semitic essays, and the Nazi regime's later embrace of his work, have cast a lasting shadow.

events.title: Elvis Presley Dies
events.blurb: A 42-year-old singer was found unresponsive on a bathroom floor of his Memphis mansion in the early afternoon and pronounced dead at a local hospital an hour later. The cause was heart failure, probably exacerbated by a cocktail of barbiturates prescribed by his personal physician. 80,000 mourners lined the four-kilometre route to the cemetery; his face had appeared on 150 magazine covers in his lifetime and would appear on tens of thousands more after his death.
events.revealBlurb: August 16, 1977 — Elvis Presley at Graceland, Memphis. An autopsy found 14 different drugs in his system. His doctor, George Nichopoulos, had his license revoked years later. "Elvis sightings" began the day after the funeral and have never entirely stopped.

events.title: Paul Simon's Graceland Released
events.blurb: A 44-year-old American songwriter released an album recorded largely in Johannesburg studios with South African musicians, fusing American folk and pop with mbaqanga, isicathamiya, and zydeco. The album was controversial: the United Nations had called for a cultural boycott of the apartheid regime, and many considered the recording sessions a violation. The finished record was nonetheless a critical and commercial phenomenon and was credited with exposing mass audiences to South African musical traditions.
events.revealBlurb: August 25, 1986 — Paul Simon. Collaborators included Ladysmith Black Mambazo, Ray Phiri, and the Boyoyo Boys. Simon was blacklisted by the UN but sang in Zimbabwe and Zambia; Nelson Mandela later thanked him for the cultural bridge.

events.title: Spotify Launches
events.blurb: A Swedish music-streaming service, developed in Stockholm and Stockholm alone for two years, launched invitation-only to users in six European countries. The service offered an enormous music library — eventually over 100 million tracks — free with ads or $10/month without. It would restructure the entire music business: album sales collapsed, streaming became the default, and royalties flowed through aggregation models that artists found miserly.
events.revealBlurb: October 7, 2008 — founded by Daniel Ek and Martin Lorentzon. The service arrived in the U.S. in July 2011 after lengthy negotiations with major labels. It had 620 million monthly active users as of 2024 — the largest audio subscription service ever.

events.title: Beyoncé's Lemonade Released
events.blurb: A 34-year-old singer dropped a surprise sixth studio album, released simultaneously with a 65-minute accompanying visual film that aired on a premium cable channel. The album and film explored, over 12 tracks, themes of infidelity, race, and Black Southern heritage. It debuted at number one on the Billboard 200 and became the only album to receive the highest score possible from Metacritic at the time. The cultural moment was so saturating that a vegetable-based cocktail name briefly came into common use.
events.revealBlurb: April 23, 2016 — Beyoncé. Film featured collaborators including Warsan Shire (poetry) and Kahlil Joseph (co-direction). The Tidal-exclusive release infuriated fans of other streaming services and drew attention to Jay-Z's struggling platform.

events.title: Hippocratic Oath Composed
events.blurb: Greek medical writers associated with a physician teaching on an Aegean island composed a short ethical oath addressed to Apollo and Asclepius, binding physicians to care for their patients, respect their teachers, preserve patient confidences, and do no harm. The document is arguably the oldest surviving code of professional ethics. Modern versions, substantially modified, are still sworn by many medical-school graduates.
events.revealBlurb: c. 400 BCE — attributed to Hippocrates of Kos, though probably composed by his students or school. The modern "first, do no harm" is actually not in the original Greek text; it appears later in Hippocrates' Epidemics. The oath still shows up at white-coat ceremonies.

events.title: Lister's Antiseptic Surgery
events.blurb: A 38-year-old Scottish surgeon, having read Pasteur's papers on germ theory, began applying carbolic acid (phenol) to his surgical wounds, instruments, and operating theatre in an effort to kill microorganisms. Mortality rates on his ward dropped from 45 to 15 percent. He published his results in a British medical journal, where they met initial resistance; adoption was slow because many surgeons resented the assertion that their own unwashed hands were killing their patients.
events.revealBlurb: August 12, 1865 — Joseph Lister at the Royal Infirmary, Glasgow. His procedures were grudgingly adopted over the next two decades. Listerine mouthwash, introduced 1879, was named after him but was not his invention. He was knighted in 1883 and made a baron in 1897.

events.title: Ross Identifies Malaria Vector
events.blurb: A 40-year-old British army medical officer working in colonial India dissected an Anopheles mosquito that had fed on a patient with malarial fever and observed the malaria parasite's oocysts developing in the mosquito's stomach wall. He had been pursuing the mosquito-borne hypothesis, championed by his mentor in London, for years. The discovery transformed tropical-disease prevention into an enterprise of draining swamps and destroying mosquito breeding sites.
events.revealBlurb: August 20, 1897 — Ronald Ross in Secunderabad, India. He called it his "mosquito day." Ross won the 1902 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. The mentor who had championed the mosquito hypothesis, Patrick Manson, was quietly robbed of credit at the time but is now recognized as a co-founder of tropical medicine.

events.title: Fleming Discovers Penicillin
events.blurb: A 47-year-old Scottish bacteriologist returning from a summer holiday to his London laboratory noticed that one of the staphylococcus-culture plates he had left stacked on his bench had been contaminated by a mold, and that a clear zone of inhibition around the mold showed the bacteria had died there. He identified the mold genus, isolated an anti-bacterial substance it produced, and published his findings — which were largely ignored for over a decade.
events.revealBlurb: September 28, 1928 — Alexander Fleming at St Mary's Hospital, London. Howard Florey and Ernst Chain at Oxford successfully purified penicillin in 1941, making it a usable drug. They shared the 1945 Nobel with Fleming. The drug's mass production during WWII saved hundreds of thousands of Allied soldiers' lives.

events.title: HIV Identified
events.blurb: A research team at a Paris institute published a paper in the journal Science describing a new retrovirus, isolated from a lymph node of a patient with lymphadenopathy, which they believed to be the cause of AIDS. A parallel American team would publish a similar finding a year later; the credit dispute between the labs lasted years and contributed to delayed public health responses. The virus had probably crossed into humans from chimpanzees in central Africa in the early 20th century.
events.revealBlurb: May 20, 1983 — Françoise Barré-Sinoussi, Luc Montagnier at Institut Pasteur. Robert Gallo at the US National Cancer Institute made a similar claim in 1984. The French were eventually credited as discoverers and won the 2008 Nobel. 40 million people have died of AIDS; antiretroviral therapy since 1996 has made it a manageable chronic disease.

events.title: Copernican Heliocentric Model Published
events.blurb: A six-volume astronomical treatise placed the Sun rather than the Earth at the centre of the universe, arguing that Earth was just one of several planets orbiting the Sun and that Earth's own daily rotation explained the apparent motion of the stars. The author received the first printed copy on the day he died.
events.revealBlurb: 1543 — Copernicus sat on the manuscript for years, fearing ridicule. A colleague secretly arranged its publication; legend holds the author held the final printed pages on his deathbed. The Church placed the book on its Index of Forbidden Books 73 years after publication — once it actually started to threaten orthodoxy.

events.title: Electromagnetic Field Equations Published
events.blurb: A Scottish physicist unified electricity, magnetism, and light into a single mathematical framework of four equations, showing that changing electric fields produce magnetic fields and vice versa — generating self-propagating waves that travel at the speed of light. The equations predicted that light was an electromagnetic wave and implied the existence of radio waves, infrared radiation, and other forms not yet observed.
events.revealBlurb: 1865 — James Clerk Maxwell's paper was read to the Royal Society in December 1864. Heinrich Hertz experimentally confirmed the existence of radio waves in 1887, nine years after Maxwell died of cancer at 48. Richard Feynman called Maxwell's equations "the most significant event of the 19th century" — a bold statement given the century's competition.

events.title: Helium Detected in the Sun
events.blurb: During a total solar eclipse, a French astronomer studying the spectrum of light from the Sun's outer atmosphere found a bright yellow spectral line that matched no known element on Earth, suggesting the existence of a new element present in the Sun but not yet found on our planet. Two months later, an English astronomer independently identified the same line and gave the element its name, derived from the Greek word for the Sun.
events.revealBlurb: August 18, 1868 — Janssen realised during the eclipse that the bright chromospheric lines could be observed in daylight without an eclipse and invented the spectroscope for doing so. Helium was not detected on Earth for another 27 years, when it was found in a uranium mineral in 1895. It is the only element discovered in space before being found on Earth.

events.title: X-Rays Discovered
events.blurb: While experimenting with cathode ray tubes in a darkened laboratory, a German physicist noticed that a fluorescent screen across the room glowed even though it was shielded from the tube's visible light. The mysterious new rays penetrated cardboard, wood, and flesh, but were blocked by dense metal. Within weeks he had produced the first medical radiograph, showing the bones of his wife's hand.
events.revealBlurb: November 8, 1895 — Wilhelm Röntgen kept the discovery secret for seven weeks, repeating every experiment before telling anyone. He named the rays "X" because he didn't know what they were. He won the very first Nobel Prize in Physics in 1901 and donated the prize money to his university.

events.title: Pluto Discovered
events.blurb: A young farm-hand-turned-astronomer at an Arizona observatory found a faint, slowly moving point of light by comparing photographic plates taken several days apart — a new body at the edge of the solar system. The discovery completed a decadelong search for a hypothetical ninth planet believed to be perturbing the orbits of the outermost known worlds.
events.revealBlurb: February 18, 1930 — Clyde Tombaugh was 24 and had never attended university. The name "Pluto" was suggested by Venetia Burney, an 11-year-old girl in Oxford, via her grandfather. In 2006, the International Astronomical Union reclassified Pluto as a "dwarf planet," prompting widespread public outrage and several state legislatures to pass resolutions disagreeing.

events.title: Metropolis Released
events.blurb: A 36-year-old Austrian director released a 153-minute silent epic — at the time the most expensive film ever made — set in a stratified future city where wealthy elites enjoy skyscraper gardens above an underground inferno of machine-tending workers. The film's visual language — robot maidens, neon skylines, expressionist sets — shaped science-fiction imagery for the next century. The premiere had uneven reception; 40 minutes of footage were later cut.
events.revealBlurb: January 10, 1927 — Fritz Lang at the UFA-Palast am Zoo, Berlin. A reasonably complete version was pieced together only in 2008, when a 16mm print from the 1930s was found in a Buenos Aires archive. The robot Maria was voted the most important film robot in history.

events.title: Rashomon Released
events.blurb: A 40-year-old Japanese director released a 88-minute film in which the same violent encounter is recounted by four different participants, none of whom agrees with any of the others. The Venice Film Festival awarded it the Golden Lion the following year, and the world film industry discovered Japanese cinema as a major force. The very title became an English noun: "the Rashomon effect" is the concept of contradictory memories.
events.revealBlurb: August 26, 1950 — Akira Kurosawa. The producers were reportedly baffled by the script and wanted it re-edited. Its Venice win completely blindsided Japanese critics, who had not thought much of the film. It led directly to the global reception of Ozu, Mizoguchi, and Kurosawa's later work.

events.title: Pather Panchali Released
events.blurb: A first-time director shot a Bengali village drama across three years in fragments whenever he could afford to — including pawning his wife's jewellery to finish an opening sequence of a boy chasing a train through tall grass. It won a Humanist Prize at Cannes and launched a tradition of realist Indian cinema that bypassed Bombay entirely.
events.revealBlurb: August 26, 1955 — Satyajit Ray's debut. He was a commercial illustrator with no directing experience; the crew were mostly amateurs. The score was composed by an then-obscure sitarist named Ravi Shankar, recorded in a single 11-hour session. The West Bengal government funded its completion after seeing rough footage.

events.title: Fellini's 8½ Released
events.blurb: An Italian director released a semi-autobiographical film about a filmmaker suffering a creative block while preparing his next picture, in which the director's own memories, dreams, and erotic fantasies dissolve into the plot he is trying to construct. The Italian title referred literally to the number of films the director had made. It won two Oscars and became the classic film-about-film-making, endlessly quoted by later directors similarly stuck.
events.revealBlurb: February 14, 1963 — Federico Fellini, with Marcello Mastroianni as his alter ego. Fellini had genuinely been blocked after a string of successes; the film emerged from trying to work out why. It was remade as a Broadway musical ("Nine") in 1982.

events.title: Titanic Released
events.blurb: A Canadian director released a 195-minute romantic epic about a fictional couple aboard the 1912 maiden voyage of the British ocean liner. The production had been the most expensive in Hollywood history, its budget having doubled during filming; industry wags predicted financial disaster. The film ran in theatres for ten months, won 11 Oscars, and became the first film to gross over a billion dollars. Its director famously shouted "I'm king of the world" from the podium.
events.revealBlurb: December 19, 1997 — James Cameron, starring Leonardo DiCaprio and Kate Winslet. It grossed $2.2 billion; Cameron's subsequent "Avatar" beat it 12 years later, also directed by him. Celine Dion's "My Heart Will Go On" spent three weeks at #1.

events.title: Machiavelli Writes The Prince
events.blurb: An unemployed former Florentine civil servant, exiled from the city after a change of regime, wrote a compact political treatise in the form of advice to a hereditary ruler on how to acquire and maintain power. Its flat, unsentimental analysis of the uses of cruelty, deception, and popular love versus fear shocked readers and made its author's name a by-word for cynical politics. It remained unpublished until five years after his death.
events.revealBlurb: 1513 — Niccolò Machiavelli. The treatise was dedicated to Lorenzo de' Medici, who almost certainly never read it. Published 1532 and promptly placed on the Papal Index of Prohibited Books in 1559. Still in print 500 years later.

events.title: Paradise Lost Published
events.blurb: A blind 58-year-old English poet, dictating to a rotating cast of scribes, completed a 10-book (later 12-book) epic poem retelling the Biblical account of the fall of man from the perspective of a sympathetically characterized Satan. Having narrowly escaped execution for his political writings under the restored monarchy, he was paid ten pounds for the manuscript. It would become the template for English epic poetry.
events.revealBlurb: 1667 — John Milton. He had gone blind in 1652 from untreated glaucoma. His daughters had to be taught to read — including Hebrew, Greek, and Latin — just so they could transcribe his dictations. "The mind is its own place..." is from Book I.

events.title: Alice in Wonderland Published
events.blurb: A 33-year-old Oxford mathematics don who had developed a story three years earlier during a boating trip with three little girls, the daughter of the dean of his college, published a book-length expansion of it. The nonsense-logic adventures of a curious girl falling into a subterranean world of mad tea parties, playing-card royalty, and cat grins without cats became the foundation text of modern children's literature.
events.revealBlurb: July 4, 1865 — Charles Dodgson, pen name Lewis Carroll. Alice Liddell was the model; their rowboat trip on July 4, 1862 was three years earlier to the day. The 1862 handwritten original, illustrated by Carroll, was given to Alice; it is now in the British Library.

events.title: First Nobel Prize in Literature
events.blurb: A Swedish Academy of cultural grandees, following the will of the dynamite inventor who had died five years earlier leaving his fortune to fund annual prizes, selected a 62-year-old French poet as the first recipient of their literature award. Their choice was safe, genteel, and now obscure; they had passed over Leo Tolstoy, widely considered Europe's greatest living novelist. The omission has dogged the Nobel Literature Prize's reputation ever since.
events.revealBlurb: December 10, 1901 — Sully Prudhomme. Other early laureates passed over: Tolstoy, Chekhov, Ibsen, Zola, Mark Twain. The prize included 150,782 Swedish kronor — a substantial sum in 1901, about $3.5 million today.

events.title: Harry Potter First Book Published
events.blurb: A 32-year-old single mother who had drafted most of the manuscript in Edinburgh cafés over six years, on single-parent benefits, published her first novel after twelve rejections from other publishers. The first print run was 500 copies; 300 went to libraries. Children started reading, telling friends, and returning. Within four years the series had become the most successful in publishing history; she would become the first novelist to reach a billion-dollar net worth.
events.revealBlurb: June 26, 1997 — J.K. Rowling, "Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone" (US title: "Sorcerer's Stone"). Her publisher Bloomsbury suggested using "J.K." instead of Joanne because boys might not read a book by a woman. The series has sold over 600 million copies.

events.title: Partition of Bengal
events.blurb: A British viceroy, citing administrative efficiency, split a vast eastern province of colonial India into two along religious lines — a Muslim-majority east and a Hindu-majority west — over the fierce protests of its Bengali elite. Boycotts of British goods, the Swadeshi movement, and targeted assassinations followed. The partition was reversed six years later, but the communal logic it had introduced could not be uninvented.
events.revealBlurb: October 16, 1905 — announced by Lord Curzon. Rabindranath Tagore led Hindus and Muslims in tying rakhis on each other's wrists in protest. The reunification in 1911 coincided with moving the colonial capital from Calcutta to Delhi.

events.title: Jallianwala Bagh Massacre
events.blurb: A British brigadier-general marched 50 rifle-armed soldiers into a walled garden in a Punjabi city where thousands of Sikhs, Hindus, and Muslims had gathered for a spring harvest festival. Without warning, he ordered ten minutes of continuous fire into the unarmed crowd, ceasing only when ammunition ran low. Official counts put the dead at 379; Indian sources gave over 1,000. He was celebrated in parts of British society as a saviour of empire.
events.revealBlurb: April 13, 1919 — Amritsar, Baisakhi day. Brigadier-General Reginald Dyer. The poet Rabindranath Tagore renounced his British knighthood in protest. A young Sikh named Udham Singh, who was at the garden that day, assassinated the former lieutenant-governor responsible for the region 21 years later in London.

events.title: Quit India Movement
events.blurb: After the failure of a British mission that offered only a vague promise of post-war dominion status, the Congress party launched a mass movement demanding immediate British withdrawal. The entire leadership was arrested at dawn the following day. The movement went underground and continued for years — sabotage, strikes, alternative governments in remote districts. It was violently suppressed, but British rule was visibly over as a legitimate proposition.
events.revealBlurb: August 8, 1942 — Gandhi's "Do or Die" speech at the Bombay Congress session. Churchill imprisoned 100,000 activists and held the line; by VJ Day in 1945, however, Britain was bankrupt and the political capital to hold India was gone.

events.title: Indian Independence & Partition
events.blurb: At the stroke of midnight, two new independent dominions came into existence on the subcontinent — one majority-Hindu, one majority-Muslim — as the British flag was lowered on the largest and oldest of Britain's imperial possessions. The division of provinces along religious lines displaced between 10 and 20 million people, and perhaps a million died in the communal violence that followed.
events.revealBlurb: August 14-15, 1947 — Pakistan on the 14th, India on the 15th. The boundary lines had been drawn by a London barrister, Cyril Radcliffe, who had never visited the subcontinent and had 36 days to complete the task. Nehru's "Tryst with Destiny" speech was delivered at midnight from the Constituent Assembly.

events.title: Chandrayaan-3 Lunar Landing
events.blurb: An Indian robotic spacecraft, after a 40-day journey that included a series of orbit-raising maneuvers to conserve fuel, performed a successful soft landing on the Moon's south polar region — a target no previous mission had reached. India became the fourth country to land on the Moon and the first to land in the south polar region, where water ice is believed to be preserved in permanently shadowed craters.
events.revealBlurb: August 23, 2023 — 18:04 IST. The lander was called Vikram; its rover was Pragyan. The national space agency ISRO had lost its predecessor Chandrayaan-2 at this phase four years earlier. The budget of the mission was around $75 million — less than the movie Interstellar.

events.title: Declaration of Independence Adopted
events.blurb: Delegates from thirteen British colonies voted to ratify a document asserting that all men are created equal and endowed with unalienable rights, formally severing political ties with the Crown. The declaration listed 27 specific grievances against the king; most delegates signed an engrossed parchment copy nearly a month later.
events.revealBlurb: July 4, 1776 — Philadelphia. Only two men actually signed on the Fourth (Hancock and Thomson). Jefferson, Franklin, and Adams all died on July 4 — Jefferson and Adams on the same day, the 50th anniversary, within hours of each other.

events.title: Declaration of the Rights of Man
events.blurb: The French National Constituent Assembly, meeting in a recently converted royal indoor tennis court, adopted a 17-article statement of universal rights: liberty, property, security, resistance to oppression, equality before the law, presumption of innocence, freedom of speech and religion. It did not grant women the vote or abolish slavery; revolutionaries would debate those extensions for years. It was still the most sweeping such declaration any European state had ever adopted.
