events.revealBlurb: August 26, 1789 — a central drafter was the Marquis de Lafayette, the American Revolution veteran. The declaration was explicitly modeled on the U.S. Declaration of Independence; in fact, Jefferson, then in Paris as American minister, advised on its drafting. It remains part of France's constitutional law.

events.title: Haitian Revolution Begins
events.blurb: A voodoo ceremony in a wooded area of a French Caribbean sugar colony marked the coordinated signal for a mass uprising of enslaved Africans. Within ten days, plantations across the northern plain were in flames and 4,000 whites and mulattos were dead. It was the largest slave revolt in the history of the Americas and the only one that successfully established an independent state. The colony had been the richest in the Western hemisphere; it produced 40 percent of the world's sugar.
events.revealBlurb: August 22, 1791 — Saint-Domingue (now Haiti). The ceremony was at Bois Caïman, led by voodoo priest Dutty Boukman. Toussaint Louverture emerged as principal leader, though he was captured by the French in 1802 and died in a freezing French prison cell. Independence came on January 1, 1804.

events.title: The Communist Manifesto
events.blurb: A 29-year-old German-born philosopher-journalist and his 27-year-old industrialist-heir collaborator published a 23-page political pamphlet commissioned by a small London-based workers' organization. Its opening sentence — about a spectre haunting Europe — and its closing rallying cry became arguably the most politically consequential prose of the 19th century. Within three weeks, revolutions were breaking out across the continent.
events.revealBlurb: February 21, 1848 — Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels. The League of the Just commissioned it. The 1848 revolutions failed; the Manifesto didn't become widely read until the 1872 edition with a new preface. By the 20th century it had shaped the political systems of a third of humanity.

events.title: Revolutions of 1848
events.blurb: Political unrest that had been gathering over economic recession and demands for constitutional government erupted within weeks across most of the European continent, beginning with a winter insurrection in Paris that deposed the king. Vienna, Berlin, Milan, Budapest, Prague, and a dozen other capitals followed within months. Liberals, nationalists, socialists, and workers briefly shared rhetoric; conservatives reorganized and, over the following year, crushed nearly every revolt. The conservative order emerged apparently reinforced — but the political grammar of 19th-century Europe had changed.
events.revealBlurb: February-June 1848 — "The Springtime of Nations." Louis-Philippe of France fled in February; Metternich resigned in Vienna in March. Only France produced lasting regime change, and it soon produced Napoleon III's Second Empire. Karl Marx and Engels published the Communist Manifesto that same February.

events.title: Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact
events.blurb: Two ideologically opposed dictatorships stunned the world by signing a non-aggression treaty after midnight in a capital city, including a secret clause dividing neighbouring countries into separate spheres of influence like cuts of a butchered animal. Every government in Europe recalculated its position by morning.
events.revealBlurb: Signed August 23, 1939 in Moscow. The secret protocol carved up Poland, Finland, the Baltic states, and Romania between Germany and the USSR — without telling any of those countries. Stalin was so pleased he personally opened champagne. The pact lasted exactly 22 months.

events.title: Fall of Tobruk
events.blurb: A fortified port city that had withstood a nine-month siege the previous year fell to an armoured assault in a single day, yielding 33,000 prisoners — including an entire South African division — along with 2,000 vehicles, 5,000 tons of food, and enough fuel to sustain the attacking force's advance for weeks.
events.revealBlurb: June 21, 1942. Churchill learned of Tobruk's fall while meeting Roosevelt in Washington — handed a pink slip of paper mid-meeting. Roosevelt's immediate response: "What can we do to help?" He arranged 300 Sherman tanks and 100 self-propelled guns for immediate shipment. The news triggered a no-confidence vote against Churchill in the House of Commons.

events.title: Battle of Stalingrad
events.blurb: For six months, a city named after a living leader was fought over house by house, factory floor by factory floor, in temperatures reaching minus 40 degrees, as an encircled attacking force slowly starved and froze while its commander received a field marshal's baton and an order never to surrender. The first capitulation of an entire German field army in the war followed 12 days later.
events.revealBlurb: August 1942 – February 2, 1943. Of the 330,000 who entered the Stalingrad pocket, 91,000 surrendered — including 24 generals and Field Marshal Friedrich Paulus. Fewer than 6,000 of those prisoners ever returned to Germany. Hitler promoted Paulus to Field Marshal the day before surrender, noting no German field marshal had ever been taken alive.

events.title: Liberation of Paris
events.blurb: A city that had been under foreign occupation for four years erupted into street fighting as its own police force led an uprising, then fell into celebration as armoured columns rolled through its boulevards, the military governor surrendered, and a tall general delivered an emotional speech from the steps of a historic civic building to a vast and weeping crowd.
events.revealBlurb: August 25, 1944. German General Dietrich von Choltitz surrendered despite Hitler's repeated orders to destroy the city's bridges, monuments, and water system. Von Choltitz later claimed he had ignored the orders to preserve Paris; historians note he may simply have lacked the engineers and explosives. De Gaulle's famous speech began: "Paris! Paris outraged! Paris broken! Paris martyred! But Paris liberated!"

events.title: Battle of Leyte Gulf
events.blurb: Over four days, 282 warships clashed in four separate engagements across several hundred thousand square kilometres of open ocean — the largest naval battle in history by tonnage and personnel — as one navy committed virtually everything it had left to stop an invasion and the other deployed over 300 ships to press it through.
events.revealBlurb: October 23–26, 1944. Japan used its remaining fleet carriers as decoys with almost no aircraft aboard. A small force of US destroyers and escort carriers somehow bluffed a vastly superior Japanese battleship force into retreating at the Battle of Samar — one of the most improbable tactical reversals of the war. Japan also deployed kamikaze suicide aircraft in force for the first time.

events.title: Eruption of Vesuvius
events.blurb: A volcano on the Italian peninsula, dormant for centuries and believed extinct by the farmers whose vineyards clung to its slopes, erupted in a single day, burying two wealthy resort towns and their roughly 16,000 inhabitants under 6 metres of ash, pumice, and pyroclastic flow. The buried cities lay undiscovered for 1,700 years.
events.revealBlurb: August 24, 79 CE — Pompeii and Herculaneum, under Mount Vesuvius. Pliny the Younger watched from across the Bay of Naples and wrote the only eyewitness account. Volcanologists still classify massive plinian eruptions by his name.

events.title: Hindenburg Disaster
events.blurb: A German passenger airship, the largest aircraft ever flown, caught fire as it approached its mooring mast at a New Jersey naval air station, and was consumed in less than 40 seconds. 36 of the 97 people on board died, along with one ground crew member. A radio reporter's anguished live commentary — "Oh, the humanity!" — entered popular idiom.
events.revealBlurb: May 6, 1937 — Lakehurst, NJ. The reporter was Herbert Morrison; he was actually there to record for later broadcast and didn't expect to be on air. The disaster effectively killed the commercial airship industry overnight.

events.title: Exxon Valdez Oil Spill
events.blurb: An oil tanker struck a well-charted reef in an Alaskan sound after the captain left the bridge and an inexperienced third mate failed to steer back into the shipping lane. 40,000 tonnes of crude oil gushed into the pristine fjord, ultimately coating 2,100 kilometres of coastline and killing hundreds of thousands of seabirds, sea otters, and orcas.
events.revealBlurb: March 24, 1989 — Prince William Sound, Alaska. The captain, Joseph Hazelwood, had been drinking. It was the worst human-caused environmental disaster in US history until Deepwater Horizon in 2010. Oil is still found under beach gravel in the area today.

events.title: Hurricane Katrina
events.blurb: A Category 3 hurricane made landfall on the US Gulf Coast, driving a storm surge that overtopped and breached the levee system protecting a major port city lying largely below sea level. 80 percent of the city flooded; 1,392 people died. The chaotic federal response — images of thousands stranded on a sports stadium roof, bodies floating in water — inflicted lasting damage on the administration in power.
events.revealBlurb: August 29, 2005 — New Orleans, Louisiana. The Superdome housed 30,000 evacuees for five days in deteriorating conditions. The head of FEMA, Michael Brown, had previously run the International Arabian Horse Association; he resigned within two weeks.

events.title: Maui Wildfires
events.blurb: High winds from a distant hurricane drove grass fires through a historic town on a Hawaiian island, reaching speeds that outpaced emergency alerts. 102 people died — many trapped in cars attempting to flee along a single coastal road — in the deadliest US wildfire in over a century. The 19th-century whaling-era town of Lāhainā, once the kingdom capital, was almost completely destroyed.
events.revealBlurb: August 8, 2023 — Lāhainā, Maui. The outdoor warning siren network, the largest in the world, was never activated. Some survivors escaped by jumping into the Pacific Ocean and treading water for hours. Downed Hawaiian Electric lines were identified as the likely ignition source.

events.title: Emmett Till Murdered
events.blurb: A 14-year-old Black boy visiting family in a rural Southern state was abducted from his great-uncle's home in the middle of the night, tortured, shot, and thrown into a river with a cotton-gin fan tied around his neck. His mother insisted on an open-casket funeral so the world could see what had been done to her son. Photographs of the mutilated body, published in Jet magazine, galvanized a generation.
events.revealBlurb: August 28, 1955 — Money, Mississippi. His accuser, Carolyn Bryant, admitted decades later she had lied about the encounter. Her husband and his half-brother were acquitted by an all-white jury, then sold their confession to Look magazine knowing they couldn't be retried.

events.title: Birmingham Children's Crusade
events.blurb: Over several days in a notoriously segregated Alabama steel city, more than a thousand Black schoolchildren — some as young as 6 — marched out of classes in organized protest. Police commissioner Bull Connor ordered fire hoses and attack dogs deployed against them. Photographs of a teenage boy lunged at by a German shepherd appeared on front pages across the world.
events.revealBlurb: May 2-5, 1963 — Birmingham, Alabama. King agreed to use children over the objections of many advisers; they were less vulnerable to losing jobs for protesting. Within weeks, the Kennedy administration introduced what became the Civil Rights Act.

events.title: March on Washington
events.blurb: A quarter-million Americans — three-quarters Black, a quarter white — gathered between the Washington and Lincoln Memorials on the 100th anniversary summer of the Emancipation Proclamation to demand the passage of civil-rights legislation then stalled in Congress. The event's closing address, given on the steps of the Lincoln Memorial, contained a phrase repeated in eight paragraphs: "I have a dream."
events.revealBlurb: August 28, 1963. MLK's prepared text did not contain "I have a dream" — Mahalia Jackson, behind him on the dais, shouted "Tell them about the dream, Martin!" and he ad-libbed the most famous passage. The Justice Department had 4,000 troops on standby in case of violence. None was needed.

events.title: Freedom Summer Murders
events.blurb: Three voter-registration volunteers — two Jewish New Yorkers and a local Black civil rights worker — disappeared after being arrested for an alleged traffic violation, released at night, and abducted by Klansmen near a Mississippi town. Their bodies were found 44 days later, bulldozed into an earthen dam. A massive FBI manhunt — the first major civil rights intervention by the Bureau — cracked the case.
events.revealBlurb: June 21, 1964 — Philadelphia, Mississippi. James Chaney, Andrew Goodman, Michael Schwerner. The state refused to prosecute; federal civil-rights conspiracy charges netted seven convictions. The ringleader, Edgar Ray Killen, was finally convicted of manslaughter in 2005 at age 80.

events.title: Los Angeles Riots
events.blurb: Four police officers filmed beating a Black motorist named Rodney King for 81 seconds after a traffic chase were acquitted of assault by a jury with no Black members. Within hours, six days of rioting erupted across South Central Los Angeles. 63 people died, 2,383 were injured, and $1 billion in property damage was inflicted — making it the costliest civil disturbance in U.S. history.
events.revealBlurb: April 29 to May 4, 1992. King himself pleaded: "Can we all get along?" The officers were subsequently retried on federal civil rights charges; two were convicted. Korean-owned small businesses in "Koreatown" were disproportionately destroyed and inadequately protected.

events.title: Bacon's Rebellion Burns Jamestown
events.blurb: A Virginia planter named Nathaniel Bacon rallied a mixed force of frontier settlers, indentured servants, and enslaved Africans against the colonial governor and marched on the capital, burning Jamestown to the ground. The uprising — the largest armed revolt in colonial America before the Revolution — exposed deep class and racial tensions that led planters to harden the legal distinction between Black slaves and white laborers.
events.revealBlurb: September 19, 1676 — Jamestown, Virginia. Bacon died of dysentery six weeks after burning the capital, ending the rebellion without a battle. Historians argue his multiracial army scared Virginia's elite so badly they accelerated the shift to race-based chattel slavery.

events.title: Boston Tea Party
events.blurb: That winter night, some 116 colonists disguised as Mohawk warriors boarded three ships in Boston Harbor and dumped 342 chests of East India Company tea into the water, destroying approximately £10,000 worth of merchandise. The targeted destruction was a direct protest against the Tea Act, which granted the company a monopoly while taxing colonial consumers.
events.revealBlurb: December 16, 1773 — Boston Harbor. Not a single participant was ever prosecuted. Britain's furious response — the Coercive Acts, which colonists renamed the Intolerable Acts — did more to unify colonial resistance than the tea party itself. The name "Boston Tea Party" wasn't coined until decades later.

events.title: Missouri Compromise Signed
events.blurb: President James Monroe signed legislation admitting Missouri as a slave state and Maine as a free state simultaneously, preserving the Senate balance between slave and free states, and drawing an invisible line across the continent at latitude 36°30' north — prohibiting slavery in all remaining territory of the Louisiana Purchase above that line.
events.revealBlurb: March 6, 1820 — Washington, D.C. Thomas Jefferson, then 76, called the Missouri debate "a fire bell in the night" that terrified him. The 36°30' line held for 34 years before the Kansas-Nebraska Act erased it in 1854.

events.title: Dred Scott Decision
events.blurb: The Supreme Court ruled 7–2 that Dred Scott, an enslaved man who had lived in free states and territories, had no right to sue for his freedom — and that Congress had never possessed the authority to ban slavery from the territories, thereby invalidating the Missouri Compromise. Chief Justice Roger Taney further held that Black Americans, free or enslaved, were not citizens and had "no rights which the white man was bound to respect."
events.revealBlurb: March 6, 1857 — Washington, D.C. The ruling was intended to settle the slavery question definitively; instead it inflamed the North and energized the new Republican Party. Dred Scott was freed by his original owner's family two months after the decision. He died 16 months later, a free man.

events.title: Women's Suffrage Amendment Certified
events.blurb: The U.S. Secretary of State certified the ratification of the Nineteenth Amendment, prohibiting any state from denying the right to vote on account of sex. The amendment's passage followed a 72-year organised campaign that had begun at the Seneca Falls Convention in 1848, when most of its original signatories were ridiculed for the demand.

events.title: Great Fire of London
events.blurb: A blaze beginning in a baker's shop on Pudding Lane burned for four days, destroying 373 acres of the medieval city including 13,200 houses, 87 churches, and most civic buildings. The fire melted the lead roof of St. Paul's Cathedral and was visible 60 miles away, yet officially killed only six people due to rapid evacuation before the flames spread.

events.title: Krakatoa Eruption
events.blurb: An island volcano in the strait between two large Indonesian islands exploded in a series of detonations culminating in a final blast so loud it was heard 4,800 kilometres away and circled the planet four times as a pressure wave. The eruption generated tsunamis that killed 36,000 people on surrounding coasts; the resulting atmospheric dust produced red-green sunsets worldwide for years.
events.revealBlurb: August 27, 1883 — Krakatoa, Sunda Strait. The final explosion had an acoustic energy roughly equivalent to 200 megatons of TNT. The glow of the afterburn may be what Edvard Munch painted in The Scream a decade later.

events.title: Mount St. Helens Eruption
events.blurb: A Pacific Northwest volcano that had been swelling a grotesque 150-metre bulge on its north flank for two months underwent a catastrophic lateral blast triggered by an earthquake. The collapse produced the largest landslide in recorded history, flattening 600 square kilometres of forest and killing 57 people, including a stubborn innkeeper who refused to evacuate.
events.revealBlurb: May 18, 1980 — Washington State, USA. The innkeeper was Harry R. Truman, 83, who kept pets and a collection of bourbon at his lodge and became a folk hero for his refusal to leave. His body was never found.

events.title: Indian Ocean Tsunami
events.blurb: A magnitude 9.1 undersea earthquake off the western coast of Sumatra — the third-largest ever recorded — displaced so much water that tsunami waves up to 30 metres high raced across the Indian Ocean, hitting 14 countries within hours. Around 228,000 people died in Indonesia, Sri Lanka, India, Thailand, and as far away as Somalia. No warning system existed.
events.revealBlurb: December 26, 2004 — Boxing Day. A 10-year-old British girl named Tilly Smith recognized the receding tide from a school geography lesson and got her family's Phuket beach evacuated, saving around 100 lives. A basin-wide warning system was operational by 2006.

events.title: Sichuan Earthquake
events.blurb: A magnitude 7.9 earthquake struck a mountainous province of southwest China in the mid-afternoon, killing around 87,000 people, including thousands of schoolchildren when substandard school buildings collapsed while adjacent government offices stood intact. The "tofu construction" scandal triggered rare citizen protests that were sharply suppressed.
events.revealBlurb: May 12, 2008 — Sichuan Province, three months before the Beijing Olympics. An artist named Ai Weiwei spent years compiling the names of the dead children; his office was raided and he was detained.

events.title: Han Dynasty Founded
events.blurb: A former peasant who had risen through the collapsing Qin military to become a rebel general defeated his principal rival in a civil war and declared himself emperor, founding a dynasty that would rule China for four centuries. The Han synthesized Confucian political theory with Qin administrative machinery, ran the Silk Road trade with the West, invented paper, cast iron plowshares, and effectively defined the imperial Chinese civilization that would persist until 1911. The ethnic majority of modern China still calls itself "Han."
events.revealBlurb: 202 BCE — Liu Bang, posthumously Emperor Gaozu. He defeated Xiang Yu at the Battle of Gaixia. The Han dynasty is conventionally divided into the Western Han (202 BCE - 9 CE) and Eastern Han (25 CE - 220 CE), with a brief Wang Mang interregnum between.

events.title: Battle of Actium
events.blurb: Off the coast of northwestern Greece, Octavian's fleet under Marcus Agrippa met the combined ships of Mark Antony and Cleopatra. When Cleopatra's Egyptian squadron broke off and fled mid-battle, Antony abandoned his own fleet to follow her; his 19 legions on shore surrendered a week later. The last serious rival to a single ruler of Rome was gone.
events.revealBlurb: September 2, 31 BCE. Antony and Cleopatra escaped to Alexandria, where both committed suicide the following year — Antony by falling on his sword (badly), Cleopatra by asp bite (legend) or poison. Octavian kept Cleopatra's son Caesarion alive just long enough to read Caesar's will, then had him killed.

events.title: Crucifixion of Jesus of Nazareth
events.blurb: A Jewish teacher from a Galilean town, who had spent a few years preaching an apocalyptic ethical message and gathering followers, was arrested by Temple authorities in the Judean capital during a Passover festival, handed to the Roman prefect, and crucified on a charge of claiming to be "King of the Jews." He was 33. A small community of his followers, convinced he had risen from the dead three days later, carried his teachings out of Judea; within three centuries their movement was the state religion of the Roman Empire.
events.revealBlurb: c. April 3, 33 CE — Jesus of Nazareth; prefect Pontius Pilate. The precise date is debated; April 7, 30 CE is an alternative. Christianity spread slowly across the first three centuries; Emperor Constantine's 313 CE Edict of Milan ended persecution; Theodosius I made it the official Roman religion in 380 CE.

events.title: Sack of Rome by the Visigoths
events.blurb: A Visigothic king and his army, frustrated by failed negotiations with a Western Roman emperor for lands and subsidies, entered Rome itself through an unguarded gate and spent three days pillaging. It was the first time the city had been sacked since the Gauls in 390 BCE — eight centuries earlier. The city's wealth and status had made it symbolically untouchable; the shock rippled through the Mediterranean world. Pagans blamed Rome's adoption of Christianity; Augustine wrote "The City of God" partly in response.
events.revealBlurb: August 24, 410 CE — Alaric I the Visigoth. The emperor Honorius was safely in Ravenna, the western capital since 402. The historian Jerome wrote from Bethlehem: "The city which had taken the whole world was itself taken." Alaric died of illness a few months after the sack.

events.title: Battle of the Catalaunian Plains
events.blurb: A Roman general of Germanic birth led a coalition of Romans, Visigoths, Franks, Burgundians, and Alans against a massive Hunnic invasion of Gaul under their formidable king. The battle — one of the largest ever fought in antiquity — ended in an indecisive but bloody Roman-allied victory that stopped the Huns' westward expansion. The Hunnic king would die suddenly two years later on his wedding night from a burst blood vessel; his empire collapsed within a decade.
events.revealBlurb: 451 CE — Flavius Aetius (Roman) and Theodoric I (Visigoth) vs. Attila the Hun. Theodoric was killed in the battle. Attila's death in 453, on his wedding night to a Germanic princess named Ildico, was probably from an esophageal hemorrhage. His sons squabbled; the Hunnic Empire dissolved.

events.title: Spanish Flu Pandemic Begins
events.blurb: An unusually lethal strain of influenza, carried through military camps and troop ships during the final months of a world war, infected a third of the planet and killed an estimated 50 to 100 million people in three successive waves over two years. Unlike most flus, it disproportionately killed healthy young adults by triggering cytokine storms in robust immune systems.
events.revealBlurb: March 1918 — first identified at a US Army base in Kansas. It was called "Spanish" only because wartime censorship in belligerent countries suppressed coverage; neutral Spain reported it freely, so it seemed to originate there. It had nothing to do with Spain.

events.title: Great Kantō Earthquake
events.blurb: A magnitude 7.9 earthquake struck the main Japanese island at noon, as hundreds of thousands of households were preparing lunch over charcoal braziers. The fires that erupted in the collapsed wooden city were fanned by a typhoon passing offshore, merging into a single firestorm with tornadoes of flame. Around 140,000 people died; 1.9 million were left homeless.
events.revealBlurb: September 1, 1923 — Tokyo and Yokohama. A persistent false rumor that ethnic Koreans were poisoning wells led to vigilante massacres of some 6,000 Korean residents. September 1 is now Japan's Disaster Prevention Day.

events.title: Bhola Cyclone
events.blurb: A tropical cyclone with 185 km/h winds made landfall on the low-lying islands of the Bay of Bengal delta at high tide, driving a 10-metre storm surge over villages built at sea level. At least 300,000 people died, possibly up to 500,000 — the deadliest tropical cyclone in recorded history. The East Pakistan government's slow response fueled the separatist movement that led to war within months.
events.revealBlurb: November 12, 1970 — East Pakistan (now Bangladesh). The relief failure helped trigger the Bangladesh Liberation War the following March. The former Beatle George Harrison organized the Concert for Bangladesh to raise funds.

events.title: Hurricane Andrew
events.blurb: A compact Category 5 hurricane made landfall in southern Florida in the early hours of a late summer morning, its eyewall gusts reaching 280 km/h. It destroyed 63,500 houses, left 175,000 people homeless, and caused $27 billion in damage — then the costliest natural disaster in US history. Building codes across the Florida peninsula were rewritten as a direct consequence.
events.revealBlurb: August 24, 1992 — Homestead, Florida. It was the first named storm of an otherwise quiet season. Eleven insurance companies went bankrupt settling claims. For comparison, Katrina 13 years later cost over $100 billion.

events.title: Tōhoku Earthquake & Fukushima
events.blurb: A magnitude 9.1 undersea earthquake off the Pacific coast of northern Japan triggered tsunami waves up to 40 metres high that killed some 19,700 people and swamped the seawalls of a coastal nuclear plant. Three reactor cores melted down in the following days, contaminating 337 square kilometres of surrounding countryside. 165,000 people were displaced; many never returned.
events.revealBlurb: March 11, 2011 — 2:46 PM local time. The quake was so powerful it shifted Earth's axis by about 17 centimetres and shortened the day by 1.8 microseconds. The plant's operator, TEPCO, had been warned about tsunami risk years earlier and ignored it.

events.title: First Tour de France
events.blurb: A French sports newspaper, in an effort to increase circulation, organized a 2,428-kilometre bicycle race around the perimeter of France — six stages, each the length of an ultra-endurance event today, with sleep-deprived cyclists riding through the night on dirt roads with a single fixed gear. Sixty cyclists started; only 21 finished. A chimney sweep named Maurice Garin won the inaugural race over 19 days of riding.
events.revealBlurb: July 1-19, 1903 — organized by L'Auto magazine, a forerunner of L'Équipe. Garin's margin of victory was an implausible 2 hours 49 minutes. He was later stripped of his 1904 title for cheating (taking trains). The race continues annually with a couple of wartime interruptions.

events.title: Babe Ruth Sold to Yankees
events.blurb: A Boston baseball team's owner, needing cash to finance a Broadway musical he had invested in, sold the star pitcher and outfielder of his defending World Series champion team to the rival New York franchise for $100,000 cash plus a $300,000 loan secured by the team's stadium. The deal shipped the best player in baseball to the Yankees; Boston did not win another World Series for 86 years. Yankee championships followed in a cascade.
events.revealBlurb: January 3, 1920 — Red Sox owner Harry Frazee sold Ruth to the Yankees. The musical was "No, No, Nanette" (1925); its eventual success does not redeem the sale. Ruth would hit 714 career home runs, lead the Yankees to 7 pennants, and define American sport for a generation.

events.title: Mark Spitz Wins Seventh Munich Gold
events.blurb: An American swimmer won his seventh gold medal of the Munich Games by anchoring the 4×100-metre medley relay team, setting a world record in every individual event he entered. No athlete had ever won more gold medals at a single Olympic Games, and he set or broke a world record in each of his seven finals.

events.title: Munich Olympics Massacre
events.blurb: Eight armed members of a Palestinian militant group scaled the perimeter fence of an Olympic Village at a German Summer Games, broke into the Israeli team's dormitory apartments, killed two Israeli athletes on the spot, and took nine others hostage. An inept German rescue operation at the military airfield where the hostages and captors had been flown ended with all nine hostages dead along with five of the eight attackers and one German police officer. The Games were suspended for a day, then resumed; the IOC president said that "the Games must go on."
events.revealBlurb: September 5-6, 1972 — Black September. IOC president: Avery Brundage. Israel's government launched a covert years-long assassination campaign against the attack's planners, known as Operation Wrath of God and dramatized in Spielberg's Munich (2005).

events.title: Messi Wins World Cup
events.blurb: A 35-year-old Argentine forward, in his fifth and final World Cup tournament, led his team to a 3-3 draw against France in the final, then won a penalty shootout 4-2 at a Qatari stadium. He scored two of the final's goals himself, then converted his penalty. The tournament's signature absence from his glittering career — the World Cup — was at last his. It was widely described as the greatest World Cup final ever played.
events.revealBlurb: December 18, 2022 — Argentina 3-3 France (4-2 pens), Lusail Stadium, Qatar. Messi and Kylian Mbappé combined for six goals between them. Messi had already won seven Ballon d'Or awards, a record; he would win an eighth in 2023. Mbappé became the first to score a hat-trick in a World Cup final since Geoff Hurst in 1966.

events.title: Madonna's "Like a Prayer" Video
events.blurb: The music video for a 30-year-old singer's new single, featuring burning crosses, stigmata, and the singer kissing a Black saint statue coming to life, premiered during a Pepsi commercial at the start of a television special paid for by the soft-drink company. The Vatican condemned the video as blasphemous; conservative Christian groups organized boycotts; Pepsi paid the singer $5 million to sever their sponsorship deal. Her album sold 15 million copies.
events.revealBlurb: March 2, 1989 — the Pepsi commercial; the full video premiered on MTV March 3. Director Mary Lambert. The controversy gave Madonna an estimated $5 million for the Pepsi deal plus enormous free publicity; she kept the money. The album "Like a Prayer" remains her best-reviewed.

events.title: The Simpsons Premieres
events.blurb: A half-hour animated primetime sitcom about a dysfunctional yellow-skinned family in the fictional American town of Springfield premiered as a Christmas special on a fledgling US television network. The show's acerbic satire, cartoon slapstick, and unprecedented crossover appeal — with children and adults watching together — established animation as a legitimate prime-time format. It is still in production three and a half decades later, the longest-running American scripted prime-time TV series.
events.revealBlurb: December 17, 1989 — the Christmas special "Simpsons Roasting on an Open Fire" on the Fox network. Created by Matt Groening from shorts he had been making for The Tracey Ullman Show since 1987. The family was named after Groening's own family except Bart, an anagram of "brat."

events.title: Seinfeld Premieres
events.blurb: A 90-minute pilot episode titled "The Seinfeld Chronicles" aired on NBC, starring a 35-year-old New York stand-up comedian as a fictionalized version of himself and three friends navigating petty social minutiae in Manhattan. NBC had almost dropped the show; test audiences had responded coolly. A show famously about "nothing," it would run 180 episodes over nine seasons and become one of the most influential sitcoms in television history.
events.revealBlurb: July 5, 1989 — Jerry Seinfeld, Jason Alexander, Michael Richards (Julia Louis-Dreyfus joined season 2). Co-creator Larry David later made Curb Your Enthusiasm, essentially a Seinfeld-universe spinoff. The cast famously turned down $5 million per episode each to continue past season 9.

events.title: Princess Diana Dies
events.blurb: A 36-year-old former British princess and two others died in a high-speed car crash in an underpass in central Paris after their driver attempted to evade pursuing paparazzi. Her death — ten months after her divorce from the heir to the British throne — triggered a massive public outpouring of grief that caught the British monarchy off guard. Over a million bouquets of flowers were left at London's royal palaces. Her funeral a week later was watched by 2.5 billion people globally.
events.revealBlurb: August 31, 1997 — Diana, Princess of Wales at the Pont de l'Alma tunnel. Her companion Dodi Fayed and the drunk driver Henri Paul also died; bodyguard Trevor Rees-Jones survived. Elton John performed a rewritten "Candle in the Wind" at the funeral, which became the best-selling single of all time.

events.title: Furby Released
events.blurb: A battery-operated toy furry pet that could speak, move its eyes, and apparently learn English words from "Furbish" over time became the must-have Christmas gift of the season. Parents who had lived through the Cabbage Patch Kids and Tickle Me Elmo crazes of previous years went through it again. The National Security Agency banned them from their premises, reportedly out of concern that they might record classified conversations and "repeat" them.
events.revealBlurb: October 2, 1998 — Tiger Electronics. 40 million Furbys sold in the first three years. The NSA's ban was based on a misunderstanding of the toy's technology — it had no recording capability at all; "learning" was a pre-programmed script that made the toy seem to become more English-speaking over time.
